options.summary: A single, self-contained command-line executable that processes notes in a single, in-memory pass. It reads all files, builds a content graph, and renders the static site directly.

components.name: File System Scanner
responsibilities: Scans the source directory for all Markdown files to be processed.

components.name: Content Parser & Analyzer
responsibilities: Parses Markdown content from files.
Extracts metadata such as tags from front matter or inline syntax.
Identifies internal links between notes.
Builds a single, in-memory graph of all notes, tags, and their relationships.

components.name: HTML & Asset Generator
responsibilities: Renders the in-memory content graph into final HTML pages for each note.
Generates index pages, such as a list of all tags and pages per tag.
Injects backlink information into note pages.
Creates a client-side search index from the note content.
Copies static assets like CSS and JS to the output directory.

components.name: Output Writer
responsibilities: Writes all generated files (HTML, JSON index, CSS, JS) to the specified output directory.

interfaces.contract: Passes a list of Markdown file paths.
Provides a complete in-memory content graph object containing all notes, tags, links, and calculated backlinks.
Streams generated file contents (HTML, JSON, CSS) along with their destination paths.

pros: Simple architecture that is straightforward to implement and maintain.
Fast for small to medium-sized sites due to minimal I/O and all-in-memory operations.
A single executable is easy for users to distribute and run.
cons: Not scalable for very large sites as the entire content graph must fit into memory.
Difficult to implement incremental builds; the entire site is rebuilt on every run, which can be slow.
Functionality is hardcoded, making it difficult to extend or customize without modifying the core application.

risks: Performance may degrade significantly with a very large number of notes, leading to high memory consumption and slow build times.
The tightly coupled design makes it difficult to swap out specific implementations, such as the Markdown renderer or the search indexing algorithm.

options.summary: A multi-stage build pipeline where each stage communicates via intermediate files (e.g., JSON). This enables caching, incremental builds, and better separation of concerns.

components.name: Ingestion Stage
responsibilities: Reads source Markdown files and converts each into a standardized intermediate data file (e.g., JSON) containing raw content and file metadata.

components.name: Analysis Stage
responsibilities: Processes the intermediate data files to parse content, extract tags, and identify links, enriching the data files with this structured metadata.

components.name: Graph Build Stage
responsibilities: Aggregates metadata from all enriched data files to build a global site graph (links, backlinks, tag relationships) and saves it as a manifest file.

components.name: Render Stage
responsibilities: Uses the enriched data files and the global graph manifest to render final HTML pages for notes, tag pages, and the search index.

components.name: Site Assembler
responsibilities: Collects all rendered files and static assets (CSS, JS) into the final output directory.

interfaces.contract: Writes and reads intermediate structured data files (one per note) to and from a cache directory on disk.
Writes enriched structured data files that are then read by the graph builder.
Writes a single site-wide graph manifest file (e.g., JSON) that is consumed by the render stage.
Outputs generated files to a temporary build directory for final assembly.

pros: Enables efficient incremental builds by allowing the pipeline to only re-run stages for changed files.
Decoupled stages are easier to test, debug, and maintain independently.
Scales better for large sites as not all data needs to be held in memory simultaneously.
cons: More complex architecture with multiple data handoffs and potential failure points.
Increased disk I/O from reading/writing intermediate files might slow down clean builds compared to an in-memory approach.
Requires a build orchestrator or sophisticated scripting to manage the pipeline stages and dependencies.

risks: The format of the intermediate representation becomes a critical and potentially rigid internal API that is hard to change.
Correctly managing the cache state and dependencies for incremental builds can be complex and error-prone.

options.summary: A core engine that orchestrates a pipeline of configurable plugins. Functionality for parsing, transforming, and rendering content is provided by swappable plugins, allowing maximum customizability.

components.name: Core Build Engine
responsibilities: Manages the overall build lifecycle and pipeline execution.
Loads and configures plugins based on user settings.
Provides a stable API for plugins to interact with the build process.

components.name: Central Data Store
responsibilities: Provides an in-memory collection of all content nodes (notes, assets, tags).
Exposes a formal API for plugins to create, read, update, and query nodes.

components.name: Parser Plugins
responsibilities: Read source files (e.g., Markdown with specific flavors) and add corresponding nodes to the Central Data Store.

components.name: Transformer Plugins
responsibilities: Manipulate the data store by adding new information, such as resolving links, adding backlinks, or creating tag indexes.

components.name: Renderer Plugins
responsibilities: Generate final output files (e.g., HTML, search index, RSS feeds) based on the final state of the Central Data Store.

interfaces.contract: The engine invokes parser plugins, providing file system access and an API to add nodes to the Central Data Store.
The engine invokes transformer plugins in a defined order, providing read/write API access to the Central Data Store.
The engine invokes renderer plugins, providing read-only API access to the Central Data Store and an API for writing output files.

pros: Extremely flexible, allowing users to support new features or syntaxes (e.g., custom Markdown extensions, different search providers) by adding plugins.
Enforces a clean separation of concerns, leading to a more maintainable core codebase.
A rich plugin ecosystem can be developed and shared by the community.
cons: Significantly more complex to design and implement the core engine and a stable plugin API.
Potential for performance overhead from plugin loading, API calls, and coordination.
Poorly written or conflicting plugins can introduce instability, security vulnerabilities, or hard-to-debug behavior.

risks: Defining a stable, powerful, and easy-to-use plugin API is a major technical challenge.
Managing dependencies and ensuring compatibility between different third-party plugins can be difficult for end-users.
The execution order of transformer plugins can have subtle and complex effects, making a build's behavior difficult to predict or reason about.
